principle: Every figure is copied from a cited publication. Cards are never averaged into a single true net cost or benefit.

assumptionAxes.label: Time frame
assumptionAxes.help: Static studies add up one year or a historical window. Dynamic studies project a lifetime NPV. They are not the same question.

assumptionAxes.label: Average vs marginal
assumptionAxes.help: Average allocates a share of existing public goods to every person. Marginal asks what extra spending an extra person causes. MAC Table 11 varies this.

assumptionAxes.label: Public goods counted
assumptionAxes.help: Defence, debt interest and ‘pure’ public goods are the usual disagreement. MAC Table 11 reports Pure public goods MC=0 and Congestible public goods MC=0 as sensitivities on the same 2022/23 groups.

assumptionAxes.label: Who is counted
assumptionAxes.help: Whole-stock EEA/non-EEA totals, recent arrivals, and visa-route cohorts answer different questions. They must not be added together.

estimates.title: EEA immigrants, all resident, 1995–2011
estimates.headline: +£4.4 billion
estimates.perAnnumNote: Migration Observatory Table 1 also quotes +£259 million a year.
estimates.methodNote: Static accounting of revenues and expenditures attributable to immigrants vs natives over the window. Journal revision of the 2013 CReAM discussion paper — the two vintages disagree in magnitude.
estimates.via: Migration Observatory, The fiscal impact of immigration in the UK, Table 1 (updated 23 June 2026)

estimates.title: Non-EEA immigrants, all resident, 1995–2011
estimates.headline: −£118 billion
estimates.perAnnumNote: Migration Observatory Table 1 also quotes −£6.9 billion a year.
estimates.methodNote: Same static framework as the EEA row. Non-EEA households in the study window were more likely to have dependent children, which raises education and family-benefit allocations.

estimates.title: Recent EEA arrivals, 2001–2011
estimates.headline: +£20.2 billion
estimates.perAnnumNote: Migration Observatory Table 1 also quotes +£1.68 billion a year.
estimates.methodNote: Same paper, restricted to immigrants who arrived after 1999. Recent arrivals are younger and cheaper to educate in the snapshot — not a lifetime result.

estimates.title: Recent non-EEA arrivals, 2001–2011
estimates.headline: +£5.2 billion
estimates.perAnnumNote: Migration Observatory Table 1 also quotes +£0.43 billion a year.
estimates.methodNote: Same recent-arrival cut as the EEA row. Sign flips versus the all-resident non-EEA total for 1995–2011 — a reason published headlines disagree.

estimates.title: EEA immigrants, 1995–2011 (discussion paper)
estimates.headline: +£8.8 billion
estimates.methodNote: Working-paper vintage of the same authors. Migration Observatory lists it separately from the 2014 Economic Journal figures. The gap (+£8.8bn vs +£4.4bn) is an assumption/revision difference, not a new official series.

estimates.title: EEA migrants, FY 2016/17
estimates.headline: +£4.7 billion
estimates.methodNote: One-year static snapshot. Not official statistics. Included because Migration Observatory Table 1 uses it to show how the same EEA/non-EEA split changes with year and method.

estimates.title: Non-EEA migrants, FY 2016/17
estimates.headline: −£9.0 billion
estimates.methodNote: Same Oxford Economics snapshot as the EEA +£4.7bn row. A one-year stock total is not a MAC visa-route lifetime NPV.

estimates.title: Recent EEA arrivals, 2001–2011 (re-estimate)
estimates.headline: −£0.3 billion
estimates.methodNote: Civitas re-working of the Dustmann–Frattini window. Same years and a similar population, opposite sign to DF 2014’s +£20.2bn recent-EEA total — the briefing’s exhibit of assumption dependence.

estimates.title: Recent non-EEA arrivals, 2001–2011 (re-estimate)
estimates.headline: −£29.7 billion
estimates.methodNote: Same Rowthorn re-estimate. DF 2014’s recent non-EEA figure for the same window is +£5.2bn.

estimates.title: EEA migrants, FY 2014/15
estimates.headline: −£1.1 billion
estimates.methodNote: Campaign-group static estimate listed by Migration Observatory to show the same EEA stock can be scored negative once public-goods and household allocations change.

estimates.title: Non-EEA migrants, FY 2014/15
estimates.headline: −£15.6 billion
estimates.methodNote: Same Migration Watch 2016 snapshot as the EEA −£1.1bn row.

estimates.title: Primary deficit, 245k vs 129k net migration, 2072/73
estimates.headline: 1.1 percentage points of GDP lower
estimates.group: ONS net-migration variants, not a visa cohort
estimates.methodNote: Age-specific tax and spend profiles applied to population projections. This is a debt-path scenario, not a £ net fiscal balance for ‘immigrants’. Higher migration does not prevent modelled debt from rising.
estimates.via: Migration Observatory briefing (23 June 2026), citing OBR 2023 long-run scenarios (245,000 vs 129,000 annual net migration).
estimates.license: OGL v3.0 (OBR) / cite Migration Observatory for the quotation

estimates.title: Debt-to-GDP, higher vs lower net migration, 2072/73
estimates.headline: about 30 percentage points lower — and still rising
estimates.methodNote: Same OBR vintage. Migration Observatory: higher net migration reduces debt as a share of GDP by 30 percentage points by 2072/73 but does not prevent debt rising from around 100 to 300 percent of GDP. OBR (2013) called this delaying, not resolving, ageing pressures.
estimates.license: OGL v3.0 (OBR) / cite Migration Observatory for the quotation

estimates.title: If public-service spend scales with population, 2028/29
estimates.headline: +£6.1 billion extra spend
estimates.methodNote: OBR 2024 five-year forecast note, as quoted by Migration Observatory: if government adjusted spending on public services to the higher-migration population, that would require an additional £6.1 billion in 2028/29. This offsets part of extra tax — it is not a net ‘cost of immigration’ stock total.
estimates.license: OGL v3.0 (OBR) / cite Migration Observatory for the quotation

estimates.title: Partner route (Family visa), 2022/23 cohort, lifetime NPV
estimates.headline: −£5.6 billion (−£109,000 per applicant)
estimates.group: Partner route of the Family visa
estimates.methodNote: MAC in-house dynamic model. Arrival-year static estimate for the same cohort is about −£30 per person — the lifetime sign is driven by ILR, ageing, and earnings, not by that first-year snapshot. Not the whole migrant stock.

estimates.title: There is no single correct estimate
estimates.headline: Pre-Brexit static studies: typically within ±1% of GDP
estimates.methodNote: Secondary evidence review. The briefing’s Table 1 is why this panel exists: four studies of 2001–2011 EEA/non-EEA groups disagree in sign once children, public goods, and ‘recent vs all resident’ change.
estimates.via: Migration Observatory key points and Table 1
